fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: Four Hours, Three Incidents
fieldNotes.source: L&D audit at a 500-person services firm, Pune (financial services vertical)
fieldNotes.story:
On April 8, 2025, the Chief People Officer of a 500-person Pune services firm rolled out a **mandatory annual 4-hour AI ethics training**. The format: a vendor-built e-learning module with seven scenarios, three quizzes, and a printable certificate. Completion was tied to the December performance cycle. By July, **98% completion**. The CPO had a slide for the board.

Between August 2025 and February 2026 the firm had **three AI-related incidents** that triggered internal review:

1. **August** — a senior consultant pasted a client's redacted-but-not-quite contract into ChatGPT to summarise it. Client name was in the metadata.
2. **November** — a manager used an AI tool to draft a performance improvement plan and forgot to remove the placeholder *"[insert weakness here]"* before sending.
3. **February** — a partner shared a board-deck draft, generated by an internal RAG tool, that hallucinated a competitor revenue number; it almost shipped to the actual board.

All three incident-causers had completed the 4-hour training. All three certificates were on file. The post-mortem, written by the new VP-People, contained one sentence in bold: *"Annual training does not change weekly behaviour."* The 2026 plan replaced the e-learning module with **weekly 20-minute team sprints**, owned by line managers, with one recent real-world scenario per week. Six months in: zero incidents.
fieldNotes.takeaway: Once-a-year training tests *memory*. Weekly sprints change *habits*. AI risk is a habits problem, so train like it.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: The Annual vs. Weekly Decision
bossBattle.setup:
**Week 20.** The HR Head, Sneha, just emailed Rajiv a shiny one-pager: *"Annual AI Ethics & Safety Training Programme — 4 hours, vendor-led, mandatory, perfect for the December cycle."* The vendor quote is ₹38 lakh. Sneha has already shown the deck to two partners.

Rajiv pings you.

*"Coach, this is exactly what the field-note Pune firm did. But Sneha's already half-sold to the partners. How do I redirect this without making her look bad?"*

coach.name: Org-Design-Veteran Omkar
coach.role: Org-design veteran, has watched seven annual training programmes fail before lunch

stages.prompt: Omkar leans back. *"Rajiv, the partners are already reading Sneha's deck. What's your opening move?"*

options.label: Approve the annual training. It's mandatory anyway, ticks the compliance box, and we can layer something better on top later.
options.explain: *"Layer something on later"* is how organisations end up with mandatory training *and* no behaviour change. The Pune firm had 98% completion and three incidents. Compliance and effectiveness are different problems.

options.label: Propose a hybrid: keep a 90-minute annual *baseline* for compliance, replace the rest with weekly 20-minute team sprints owned by line managers.
options.explain: **Correct.** You preserve Sneha's compliance need *and* fix the behaviour-change gap. Omkar: *"You gave her a win and the firm a better outcome. That's how you redirect without burning a peer."*

options.label: Kill the annual training entirely. It's bad and we should say so.
options.explain: You'd be technically right and politically dead by the next partner meeting. Sneha walks out, the partners side with her, and your weekly-sprint idea never sees the light. Right answer, wrong delivery.

options.label: Buy two annual programmes — one ethics, one safety — to be extra thorough.
options.explain: Twice the certificates, same zero behaviour change. The Pune firm's three incidents wouldn't have been prevented by adding a fourth hour.

stages.prompt: Sneha agrees to the hybrid. She asks: *"Who runs the weekly sprints? L&D doesn't have bandwidth."* What do you tell Rajiv?

options.label: *"Hire an L&D vendor to deliver weekly sessions across all teams."*
options.explain: Vendor-delivered weekly sessions are just the annual programme served fifty-two times. The whole point is to embed in *team* context. Outsourcing the delivery defeats the design.

options.label: *"Line managers run them. 20 minutes of one real recent scenario, in the team's stand-up slot. L&D supplies the scenario library and a one-page facilitation guide."*
options.explain: **Yes.** Manager-led, in-context, scenario-driven. The team talks about *their* near-misses, not a vendor's hypotheticals. Omkar: *"Now you've turned every manager into an L&D channel. That's leverage."*

options.label: *"Make it self-paced — drop a 20-minute video in Slack every Monday and trust people to watch."*
options.explain: Self-paced video in Slack is the annual programme served as a podcast. No discussion, no team context, no behaviour change. People will mark it watched and scroll.

options.label: *"Run a peer-champion model — three trained champions per function, rotating who facilitates."*
options.explain: **Solid alternative.** Champions scale better than managers in firms where managers are stretched thin. Either model works as long as the *facilitation is local*. Pair with manager support and you're set.

stages.prompt: The CPO asks: *"How do I prove to the board this is working better than the old programme?"* Last call.

options.label: *"Completion rates. Just like before. We'll see 80%+ across teams."*
options.explain: Completion was 98% at the Pune firm. The board needs to see *behaviour* change, not attendance. Wrong metric.

options.label: *"Two metrics: incident count (lagging) and self-reported near-misses (leading). Plus a quarterly anonymous survey on confidence in handling AI scenarios."*
options.explain: **This is the move.** Lagging plus leading plus qualitative. Near-misses-reported is the gold metric — it goes *up* when training is working, because people are noticing more, not because more is going wrong. Omkar saves this in his notebook.

options.label: *"Vibes. Walk the floor, ask people what they did differently this month."*
options.explain: Walking the floor is *necessary* but not sufficient. The board needs a number. "Vibes" is what gets cut when budgets tighten.

options.label: *"Cost-per-employee training spend. Should drop 60% versus the annual programme."*
options.explain: Saving money on training is not the win. The Pune firm saved nothing and spent ₹38 lakh; the new programme will cost less *and* work better. But the board cares about outcomes, not unit costs.

outcomes.perfect: You preserved Sneha's compliance baseline, redirected the bulk into weekly team sprints, and shipped a metric that actually measures behaviour. **Omkar nods slowly. That's the correct nod.** On to Week 26.
outcomes.good: You avoided the once-a-year-tick-the-box outcome but flinched once. Re-read the lesson on **annual vs. weekly cadence** before the next L&D budget cycle.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for compliance and got the Pune firm's three incidents on paper. Re-read the lesson — 98% completion did not stop a single incident there. Your draw was a drill.
